answer.label: Not Rumi — and not Nietzsche either
answer.authorDates: Origin anonymous · oldest documented version 1813 · in print as a proverb by 1927
answer.sourceLine: There is no Rumi source. The line is not among Rumi’s sourced quotations, and the closest thing to it in any Rumi book is a different sentence from a 2004 Coleman Barks rendering. The sentence is far more often pinned on Nietzsche, and that credit fails too: Quote Investigator found no substantive evidence he used the expression and concluded that “based on current evidence the statement origin seems to be anonymous.” The oldest documented version of the image is Germaine de Staël’s, written in 1813 — and by 1927 The Times of London was already calling the saying an old proverb.

source.heading: The source

docMeta.dd: Rumi — and, far more often, Friedrich Nietzsche
Germaine de Staël · J. Murray, London, 1813
Not present among Wikiquote’s sourced Rumi quotations

source.excerpt: . . . sometimes even in the habitual course of life, the reality of this world disappears all at once, and we feel ourselves in the middle of its interests as we should at a ball, where we did not hear the music; the dancing that we saw there would appear insane.
trail: The line is not Rumi’s, and it is not Nietzsche’s either. Quote Investigator tracked the saying across nearly two centuries of print and ended where honest research usually ends on a line like this: “Based on current evidence the statement origin seems to be anonymous” the full chronology ↗.

The oldest documented version is not Persian but French. In 1813 Germaine de Staël published De l’Allemagne, known in English as Germany, and Wikiquote quotes the ball-without-music passage from it as the first recorded appearance — filed, notably, under Misattributed on its Nietzsche page Wikiquote ↗.

By 1927 the saying was already being described as old. The Times of London printed “They who dance are thought mad by those who hear not the music” and called it an old proverb; a 1936 Boston Globe column filed a near-identical wording under “Modern Proverbs” the citations ↗.

The polished modern sentence arrives late. In Quote Investigator’s chronology it appears in 2005, in a Florida newspaper’s “They Said It” column, already ascribed to Nietzsche — eight years after George Carlin printed a shorter form in Brain Droppings, and four years after he reprinted it credited simply “– Anon.” QI ↗.
source.excerptNote: This is the oldest documented version of the thought — and it is neither Rumi nor the modern wording. Germaine de Staël is describing a moment when ordinary life abruptly looks purposeless, not coining an aphorism about nonconformity. Wikiquote quotes this passage as the “first recorded appearance” of the saying.

author.name: Rumi
author.kicker: The name it gets pinned to
author.heading: Why it lands on Rumi
author.metaLine: 1207–1273 · Persian poet and Sufi mystic · the order formed around him gave the world the whirling dervishes
author.bio: Jalal al-Din Muhammad Rumi was a thirteenth-century Persian poet and Sufi mystic who settled in Konya, and the Mevlevi order that grew around him became known worldwide for the whirling sama ceremony. That association is exactly why an aphorism about dancing to music other people cannot hear drifts towards his name. His actual corpus is enormous and specific — the six-book Masnavi and the Divan-i Shams, tens of thousands of lines — and this sentence is in neither. Much of the English “Rumi” circulating online comes from modern re-renderings by writers who do not read Persian, which is how loose material ends up under his name in the first place.

misattribution.heading: Who it gets pinned on
misattribution.intro: This line is a magnet. The same thought circulates under at least four different names, and not one of them survives contact with the record.

items.why: The sentence is not among Wikiquote’s sourced Rumi quotations ↗, and Quote Investigator’s chronology contains no Rumi instance of it at all — only a thematically related passage from the 2004 expanded edition of Coleman Barks’s The Essential Rumi: “We rarely hear the inward music, but we’re all dancing to it nevertheless” QI ↗. Different sentence, different claim — and Barks’s books are re-renderings rather than translations from the Persian.

Wikiquote lists “Those who dance appear insane to those who cannot hear the music” in the Misattributed section of its Nietzsche page Wikiquote ↗, and Quote Investigator states flatly that it “has not yet located any substantive evidence that Nietzsche used this expression” QI ↗.

A variant — “Those who danced were thought to be quite insane by those who could not hear the music” — travels under the name Angela Monet. Quote Investigator reports a Colorado newspaper crediting her in 2002, and that Poetry Society staff had never heard of her: “Monet doesn’t appear to exist” QI ↗.

Carlin printed “Those who dance are considered insane by those who can’t hear the music” in Brain Droppings (1997); when the line reappeared in Napalm & Silly Putty (2001) it carried the credit “– Anon.” — he did not claim it QI ↗.

misattribution.truthLine: The honest answer is the unglamorous one: nobody knows who said it first. Quote Investigator’s verdict is that “based on current evidence the statement origin seems to be anonymous” — a saying already being called an old proverb in 1927, long before either Rumi’s or Nietzsche’s name was attached to it Quote Investigator ↗.

context.heading: Why this one spreads
lead: The sentence is built for sharing: it flatters the reader, quietly condemns everyone else, and needs no context whatsoever. That is also why it has no author. Lines like this accrete over generations of retelling, and the famous names attach afterwards — whichever name makes the sentiment feel authorised.

The paper trail runs backwards through comedy, newspapers and proverb collections to a French novelist. In 1813 Germaine de Staël described the feeling of watching a ball without hearing the music; by 1927 The Times of London was printing a compact proverb version and calling it old; by the late 1990s George Carlin had it as an anonymous one-liner; and only in the mid-2000s did the polished modern wording begin arriving with Nietzsche’s name on it — and, on social media, Rumi’s.
detailsBody: A proverb reference work quoted by Quote Investigator, the Thesaurus of Traditional English Metaphor (2002), records “they who dance are thought mad by those who hear not the music” tagged with the date 1575. No sixteenth-century text appears anywhere in QI’s own chronology, whose earliest located citation is 1813 — so read the 1575 tag as a compiler’s estimate of the proverb’s age, not as a found source QI ↗.
The modern wording got its largest single push in 2010, when Megan Fox had it tattooed on her body and the British press discussed the new tattoo — repeating the Nietzsche credit as it went QI ↗.
context.pull: It was already an “old proverb” in 1927 — long before anyone thought to put Nietzsche’s or Rumi’s name on it.
